chapter.title: Walking the site: reading what got built

cards.body:
Your builder has finished a small house. Before you pay, you walk through it. **Every small web project is the same 4 things seen from the hallway**: the walls and rooms, the paint, the wiring behind the switches, and the clipboard of permits hung by the door.

Picture a folder with 4 files in it. Each file is one of those four.
cards.simpler:
Imagine a builder just finished a small house for you. Before you pay, you walk through it. A small web project works the same way. **It is always the same 4 things seen from the hallway**: the walls and rooms, the paint, the wiring behind the switches, and the clipboard of permits by the door.

Now picture a folder with 4 files in it. Each file is one of those four things.

cards.prompt: Claude built your recipe app. The Save button works, but it's a sickly yellow-green. In house terms, which part needs attention?

options.text: The walls: where the button sits on the page
The paint: how the button looks
The wiring: what the button does when pressed

whyNot.a: That's the page, not the styling: the page decides a button exists and where it sits, not its colour.
whyNot.c: That's the logic, not the styling: the wiring handles what happens on press, and the button already works.

cards.reteach: Split any complaint into three questions. Is it there? That's the page. Does it look right? That's the styling. Does it do the right thing? That's the logic. A bad colour is a looks question.

cards.title: The rooms and the paint
cards.body:
The *page file* ends in .html, often named index.html. It is the rooms and walls: every heading, box, button and bit of text, in the order they appear on screen. If something is missing from the screen, it is missing here.

The *styling file* ends in .css, often style.css. It is the paint and fixtures: colours, sizes, fonts, spacing. It never adds a button. It only decides how the button looks.

**You can tell a file's job from its ending.** You do not need to read it yet. Just know which door you are standing at.
cards.simpler:
The page file ends in .html, often index.html. It is the rooms and walls: every heading, box, button and bit of text, in the order they appear. Missing from the screen means missing here.

The styling file ends in .css, often style.css. It is the paint: colours, sizes, fonts, spacing. It never adds a button, only decides how it looks.

**The file ending tells you the file's job.** Don't read it yet. Just know which door you are at.

cards.title: Priya's tip calculator
cards.body:
Priya asks Claude Code for a tip calculator. The folder comes back with 4 files: index.html, style.css, app.js and package.json.

She opens index.html and recognises her own words: Bill amount, Tip percent, Total. She opens style.css and finds color: #2e7d32, the green she asked for.

She opens package.json hoping to find the maths. It is 14 lines of names and version numbers. **The maths is in app.js**, line 9: total = bill + bill * percent / 100. That one line is the entire product.

cards.prompt: Your to-do app adds a task when you click Add, but pressing Enter does nothing. You want to look before asking Claude. Which file do you open first?

whyNot.a: That's the page, not the logic: index.html says there is a text box, not what happens when you press a key inside it.
whyNot.b: That's the styling, not the logic: style.css only changes how the box looks, and it looks fine.

cards.reteach: Ask what kind of problem it is. Enter doing nothing is a behaviour problem: a key was pressed and nothing happened. Behaviour lives in the wiring, the .js file. Looks live in .css. Presence lives in .html.

cards.title: The wiring and the clipboard
cards.body:
The *logic file* ends in .js, often app.js or main.js. It is the wiring and plumbing: what happens when you click, type or load the page. Any 'it does not do X' problem lives here.

The *settings files* are the builder's clipboard: package.json and anything with config in its name. They list the project's name, the tools it uses and their version numbers. You read them. You almost never edit them by hand.

**When a file makes no sense, ask the builder to read it to you.** Try: 'Explain app.js in plain words, one paragraph, no code.' Or: 'What does line 9 do, and what breaks if I delete it?'
cards.simpler:
The logic file ends in .js, often app.js or main.js. It is the wiring: what happens when you click, type or load the page. 'It does not do X' problems live here.

Settings files are the builder's clipboard: package.json and anything named config. They list the project's name, tools and version numbers. Read them. Almost never edit them by hand.

**Ask the builder to read any confusing file to you.** Try: 'Explain app.js in plain words, no code.'

cards.body:
Marcus opens package.json, sees 20 lines he does not understand, and deletes 6 of them to keep things tidy. The app will not start the next morning, and Claude needs 10 minutes to work out why.

Spot it: a file that is mostly names, quotes and numbers like 4.2.1 is settings. **Read settings, never tidy them.** If you want it shorter, ask Claude whether anything can go.

cards.prompt: Claude reports: 'I made the title bigger and moved it above the search box.' Which 2 files did it most likely change?

whyNot.b: That's the wiring and the clipboard, not looks and layout: nothing changed about behaviour or about which tools the project uses.
whyNot.c: Half right: bigger is styling, but moving the title above the search box changes the page order, not the settings.

cards.reteach: Match each word in Claude's report to a file. Bigger is a looks word, so style.css. Moved above is an order word, so index.html. Nothing here is about what happens on click, and nothing is about tools or versions.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: A small web project is 4 kinds of files: the page is the rooms, the styling is the paint, the logic is the wiring, and the settings are the builder's clipboard. **Guess the job from the file ending, then ask Claude to explain it in plain words before you touch anything.**
cards.simpler: A small web project is 4 kinds of files. The page is the rooms. The styling is the paint. The logic is the wiring. The settings are the builder's clipboard. **Guess each file's job from its ending, then ask Claude to explain it in plain words before you touch anything.**

cards.body: Open the folder from chapter 1 in Claude Code and type: 'List every file here and say in one line what each one does.' Sort its answer into rooms, paint, wiring and clipboard.
cards.simpler: Open the folder from chapter 1 in Claude Code. Type this: 'List every file here and say in one line what each one does.' When the answer comes back, **sort each file into rooms, paint, wiring or clipboard.** Use each file's ending to decide which is which.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now open a project folder, name what each main file is for, and ask Claude to explain any piece you don't follow.
